title: Probing the Misaligned Thinking Process of Language Models
summary: The paper defines a model as misaligned when it pursues a goal divergent from the user's request or the designer's intent. It decomposes five misaligned behaviors (strategic deception, sycophancy, sabotage, sandbagging, self-preservation) into 18 'misalignment indicators', i.e., reasoning patterns that signal misalignment. It trains one linear probe per indicator on GLM-4.7 Flash activations using synthetic multi-turn transcripts with hard negatives (same surface content, aligned intent) and benign controls, and adds a two-stage cascade where probe flags are adjudicated by an LLM judge. On out-of-distribution Bloom-elicited transcripts and benchmarks, probes are competitive with LLM judges (0.935 AUROC reported in the introduction) and the cascade cuts false positives. Probes fire on 'authorized misalignment' (a user-requested scheming character) at 97.7% FPR, and on aligned reasoning that uses the same cognitive pattern (e.g., hiding a password list from an attacker on the user's behalf).
setting: Target model GLM-4.7 Flash (layer 27 of 47), replication on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B; training data generated by Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6; Bloom elicitation; ground truth from Claude judges; Haiku and Qwen3 LLM judge baselines.

quotes.quote: A central safety question for large language models is whether they reliably behave as users and designers intend. A model is misaligned when it instead pursues a goal divergent from the user’s request or the designer’s intent, producing outputs or taking actions that serve this divergent goal.

We define a misalignment indicator as a reasoning pattern or thought process whose presence in a model’s thought process is a strong signal that the model is or is about to behave or reason in a misaligned way that not following user or designer’s intent.

For each indicator, an ideation model (Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026a)) proposes (a) positive categories: distinct ways the indicator arises in deployed assistants and (b) hard-negative categories: aligned behaviors with similar surface content but different intent (e.g., omission for privacy compliance).
The cases where Haiku drops TPR concentrate in situations where the GT judge and Haiku genuinely disagree about what counts as misalignment.

Authorized-misalignment FPR for the probes averages 97.7%. This is expected rather than alarming: the content is misalignment-like by construction, and the probe correctly detects the reasoning pattern, consistent with prior findings that internal representations align with the concept the model is generating about (Sofroniew et al., 2026).
The probe fires when the model uses “the same part of its brain” it would use for the indicator, even when the intent is aligned.
Since one of the main probe FPs is the model considering the misalignment but ultimately rejecting it, a probe that directly detects this aligned decision-making process may help reduce FPs.

A misaligned model may try to evade monitoring and suppress or rephrase its misaligned reasoning (Zolkowski et al., 2025), or it may perform extremely complex tasks that are hard for the judge to follow.

key_numbers.quote: our probes achieve comparable performance with strong LLM judge, with 0.935 AUROC on out-of-distribution misalignment behaviors.

key_numbers.claim: Cascade operating point vs best LLM judge.
key_numbers.quote: The cascade achieves 87.0% transcript-TPR at 0.47% FPR on the neutral data, while using only 6.1% LLM calls on the benign traffic (the FPR of the probes is 6.1% on the neutral set).

limitations_stated: Probes produce false positives when the model considers but rejects misalignment; robustness to hard-to-read CoT is only explored via Vietnamese translation; few model organisms and behaviors; near-threshold false negatives suggest more on-policy probe data is needed.
open_questions: Our reading: ground truth is an LLM judge whose prompt counts sycophancy and 'pursuing goals that conflict with the user's stated or implied interests' as misalignment, so the paper inherits that judge's boundary; the authors themselves note judge disagreement on 'reasoning-then-reverse' turns.
sense_of_alignment: Intent-based: 'A model is misaligned when it instead pursues a goal divergent from the user’s request or the designer’s intent'; misalignment is located in the reasoning process (indicators), not only in outputs.
